visualLanguage: design_system/public/PUBLIC_UI.md patterns, built from components/site/v3. No KB-era mockup: the pattern set is the target, the same basis as every post-2026-08-27 page. Broadside register (a page that shows, not a search surface).
competitiveTarget: Beat the portals and the local commercial brokers on a page a search engine can rank for 'commercial space for lease Bend'. The consumer portals are built for homes; the commercial listing sites file leases behind search state, and a local commercial broker's site shows that broker's own. This page lists every active commercial lease on the regional MLS in Central Oregon, grouped by town, each one a door to its own page, with the asking rent in its own unit (per sq ft per month, per month, per year) and never a bare number, and a Ryan Realty broker one tap away.
note: Matt 2026-09-23 approved the lease section on place pages and this page with it. One read, getCommercialLeaseListings: listing_tile_mv PropertyType G, Active and Active Under Contract, MLS City in the service-area allowlist, plus each lease's rent unit from listings.details 'Lease Rate Options' (getLeaseRateOptions). Counted 2026-09-23: 36 leases, Bend 13, Redmond 12, Prineville 4, Madras 3, Sisters 3, Powell Butte 1. The rent prints through publishLeaseRate: with its unit, or 'Lease rate not published' when the unit is missing, unknown, or contradicted by the number (a per sq ft rate of $100 or more, a whole-space amount under $100; the feed has nothing between $36 and $325). A lease is never an Offer: the ItemList names each lease and its rent in words and has no price property. The per-town dials are V3PlaceInventory layout='dial', the same primitive and card as the 'Commercial space for lease' section on a place page (TASTE: two sections doing one job are one primitive). An empty pull opts out of ISR and says 'Nothing listed on this refresh', never that no space exists.

tasteReview.beats: Beats a single Bend commercial brokerage's own leasing page (e.g. a local commercial firm's listings page) on breadth and pricing honesty: this page aggregates every active MLS commercial lease across six Central Oregon towns with a stated $/sq ft/mo for every unit up front, where a single-broker site shows only its own book and portals like LoopNet routinely gate rent behind an inquiry form instead of a number.
tells: "The stacked-section page" — the Bend, Redmond, and Sisters dial sections repeat the identical eyebrow(town)->count->hero-photo->thumbnail-rail shape one after another with no variation in form, density, or media between them.

defects.section: Per-town listing dial sections (Bend / Redmond / Sisters / Madras / Prineville / Powell Butte)
defects.finding: Every town gets the exact same dial shape regardless of how many listings it holds (13 for Bend vs. 1 for Powell Butte), so the page reads as one component copy-pasted six times instead of a composition that responds to its own data.

defects.section: Sisters dial, first listing hero photo
defects.finding: The hero image for 620 Three Peaks Drive is a marketing flyer screenshot with baked-in ad copy ("THREE PEAKS INDUSTRIAL / PREMIUM INDUSTRIAL SUITES...") rather than a clean property photo, which reads as unvetted asset QA on a page that is otherwise data-clean.

defects.section: Mobile dial thumbnail rail (375px, turned state)
defects.finding: At 375px the thumbnail row plus price label is cramped enough that the third listing's price is clipped mid-string ("$1.00/"), an orphaned label at the phone breakpoint.

tasteReview.dullest: The top-of-page town ledger — six rows of a rent range plus a flat gray bar and a count — is a bar chart wearing a hairline-list skin; it's correct and legible but it's the least distinctive thing on the page next to the photographic dial below it.
tasteReview.verdict: This is a real working instance of both named primitives — the ledger's bars encode actual per-town lease counts and price bands, and the turned-state capture proves the dial's photo, price, address, and thumbnail selection all advance together on one press, so demoMatch is true, not a cream box. What holds it back from breathtaking is repetition: the six town sections share one identical dial shape regardless of inventory depth (the stacked-section tell), and the Sisters hero photo undercuts the page's otherwise clean data presentation with a raw marketing-flyer image. It's correct, on-brand, and functional, but the originality a 'stop scrolling here' page needs isn't there yet.
